summary: The paper introduces CDAS, a steering method that combines a JSD-based distribution-matching objective with distributed interchange interventions (DII) to enable bi-directional, tuning-friendly concept control in LLMs. The design is thoughtful and motivated (linking steering to causal-variable localization rather than fine-tuning), and the safety case studies (refusal override, CoT backdoor) offer meaningful evidence. However, the headline empirical claim of a more faithful/tunefree method is only partly supported: on AxBench CDAS underperforms RePS on Gemma-2-2B and at Gemma-2-9B layer 31, its 'unit factor' advantage collapses when tuning is applied, and reporting of variance/statistical significance is thin outside Case Study 2. The contribution is interesting but currently sits at borderline-reject; substantial added experiments and clearer scoping of claims are needed.
strengths: Conceptual reframing of steering as causal-feature identification rather than parameter-efficient fine-tuning is well argued and connects steering to a growing mechanistic-interpretability literature.

The JSD distribution-matching objective plus DII protocol is a novel combination for steering, and the design rationale (avoiding overfitting to ground-truth tokens, implicit factor sampling via counterfactual inputs) is coherent.
Evaluation spans a well-chosen benchmark (AxBench) and two safety-relevant case studies at multiple model scales up to 70B, including a non-trivial CoT backdoor scenario.

Faithfulness is measured with KL divergence to the natural distribution and standard-benchmark deltas (MMLU, TruthfulQA, tinyBenchmarks), and CDAS's utility-preservation results (especially on larger LLMs) are compelling.
The paper is calibrated: authors explicitly note that CDAS does not always beat Lang./RePS and give layer-by-layer variance, which is unusually candid.

key_concerns.issue: The 'tuning-free' advantage is overclaimed. On AxBench, unit-factor CDAS is markedly weaker than tuned CDAS (e.g., 0.121 vs 0.631 on 2B/L10), and the paper still relies on β>1 grid search for competitive scores; the benefit only materializes in case studies where interventions target well-understood one-dimensional features (refusal, backdoor). This tension between the AxBench and case-study conclusions should be scoped more carefully in the abstract/intro/conclusion.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Reframe headline claims to distinguish between general-purpose steering (where CDAS needs tuning and is not SOTA) and low-dimensional safety concepts (where CDAS is competitive tuning-free). Report tuned-vs-untuned results for RePS/DIM on the case studies for symmetry.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical rigor is uneven. Case Study 2 mentions three initializations with standard error, but Table 1 (AxBench) and Table 2 (refusal) give no seeds, no error bars, and no significance tests. Some reported gaps (e.g., 0.023 layer-to-layer consistency vs RePS's 0.150) are the paper's key positive claim yet come without variance.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add multiple seeds (>=3) for AxBench and Case Study 1, report standard deviations, and perform paired significance tests (e.g., bootstrapped or Wilcoxon) between CDAS and RePS/Lang./DIM on the metrics that anchor claims.

key_concerns.issue: Baselines are asymmetrically handled. RePS gets factor tuning on both case studies, while CDAS gets unit factors — a comparison that favors CDAS on faithfulness metrics (KL, benchmark preservation) essentially by construction, because RePS is being pushed harder. Also, LoReFT is only shown as skyline on AxBench, and no fine-tuning baseline appears in case studies.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report both tuned and untuned versions of each method on each task, and include at least one fine-tuning or LoRA baseline in the case studies to contextualize the utility-preservation claim.

key_concerns.issue: Generality is under-supported. Benchmarks are restricted to Gemma-2 (2B/9B) for AxBench and Phi/Llama for case studies; no results on Qwen, Mistral, or non-instruct base models, and no cross-benchmark evaluation of interpretability properties. The paper's claim that CDAS 'may benefit from model scale' rests on two data points.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add at least one additional model family on AxBench and a broader model panel (e.g., 3-5 model families) for the refusal case study; systematically report the scaling trend.

key_concerns.issue: The Remark that 'CDAS is not causal variable localization' is important but appears late and undercuts the framing that motivates the method in the intro. Readers may find the mechanistic-interpretability framing overstated relative to what the objective actually guarantees.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Move this caveat earlier and align abstract/intro language accordingly; be explicit that CDAS is 'DAS-inspired,' not a causal-abstraction guarantee.

key_concerns.issue: Writing quality: several sentences read as machine-formatted or lightly proofread (missing spaces around punctuation, run-ons, inconsistent capitalization), which hurts the paper's clarity beyond the double-blind formatting.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Copy-edit thoroughly; tighten Section 3.3 and 4 in particular.

key_concerns.issue: Reproducibility of the CDAS-specific data augmentation (using gpt-4o-mini to generate y_i and template-based x^c_i) is described only at a high level; downstream results may be sensitive to the neutral-response distribution.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include the exact augmentation prompts/templates in the main text or appendix, and a small ablation swapping the generator model (e.g., gpt-4o-mini vs open model) to bound sensitivity.

questions_for_authors: How sensitive is CDAS to the choice of intervention token position within the chat template (currently grid-searched over <model> tokens)? Please report a full sweep for at least one setup.

Why does CDAS's advantage over RePS on utility-preservation disappear when RePS uses smaller (untuned) factors matched to CDAS's effective factor magnitude? A controlled comparison at matched intervention norms would clarify whether the faithfulness gain comes from the JSD objective or simply from smaller intervention magnitudes.

The AxBench 'oracle' vs 'fair' factor selection distinction should be defined more precisely: are both computed on the same held-out set, and are RePS/BiPO numbers comparably oracle-selected? Please clarify to avoid apples-to-oranges comparisons.

In Case Study 2, the training set (272 red-teaming instructions, largely LLM-augmented from 7 seeds) risks distributional overlap with the held-out evaluation. What is the semantic diversity of the held-out red-teaming set relative to training?
Have you tried other f-divergences (forward/reverse KL, TV) in place of JSD? The choice is well motivated conceptually but not empirically compared.

Beyond rank-1, does the CDAS objective remain stable at higher rank, or does the distribution-matching signal become too weak? Even a preliminary rank-2/4 result would substantiate the future-work claim.
calibration_check: Claims are largely scoped honestly (authors explicitly note that CDAS 'may not always outperform' Lang./PO methods), but the 'tuning-free' framing and the notion of 'systematic control' are stronger than the mixed AxBench and Case Study 1 numbers actually support.

significance.justification: Adds a distinct point in the steering design space and produces useful utility-preservation results, but the practical takeaway ('use CDAS when big models or utility matters, otherwise RePS') is narrow and unlikely to shift community practice broadly.

novelty.justification: The JSD distribution-matching + DII combination is a genuinely new steering objective, though it inherits heavily from DAS and existing distribution-matching work; the novelty is in the composition, not in a new mechanism.

rigor.justification: Method derivation and motivations are sound, but the empirical link between the causal-feature framing and the observed results is weakened by the Remark that CDAS is not actually a causal-localization method; several claims are supported by only 1-2 data points.

statistical_soundness.justification: Only Case Study 2 uses three seeds with standard error; AxBench and Case Study 1 lack seeds, error bars, or significance tests, so several central comparisons (e.g., layer-to-layer consistency, RePS vs CDAS on larger models) are not statistically anchored.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper is unusually candid about limitations (mixed AxBench results, need for factor tuning, non-rigorous causal grounding), though headline framing ('faithful,' 'systematic control') still runs somewhat ahead of the evidence.

clarity.justification: Overall argument is followable, but the manuscript has visible formatting issues, awkward phrasing, and the crucial Remark on CDAS's scope arrives late; Section 3.3 needs tightening.

structure_compliance.justification: Follows a standard ICLR structure (intro, related work, method, benchmark, case studies, conclusion) and fits within a reasonable length; sections are well delineated.

reproducibility.justification: Core method is described with sufficient formalism, and AxBench is a public benchmark, but crucial details (augmentation prompts, red-teaming construction, seed counts, exact hyperparameter grids) are relegated to appendices and only summarized here.

related_work.justification: Covers steering-vector, causal-abstraction, distribution-matching, and safety-mechanism literatures reasonably, though positioning against SAE-based steering and other 2024/2025 optimization-based steering work could be sharper.

figure_quality.justification: Tables are informative but text-formatting artifacts make them hard to parse from the extraction; Figure 1's ASR-vs-layer plots directly support the case-study claim, but display-item captions elsewhere are terse.

breadth_generality.justification: AxBench uses only Gemma-2 (2B, 9B); case studies use Phi and Llama-3.1, but no other families and limited benchmarks per case study, which is thin support for the claimed model-scale advantage.

overall_recommendation.justification: Interesting, well-motivated method with candid limitations, but mixed empirical results, asymmetric baseline treatment, and thin statistical reporting keep it below the ICLR acceptance bar in its current form.
